newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila shares suffer on peso fears.
newsitem.headline: Manila shares suffer on peso fears.

text.p: Philippine shares hit a two-month closing low on Thursday after being pummelled for the second consecutive day, and analysts said only an end to the speculation on the peso could calm the market.

"High interest rates and that's the one reason the market is moving this way. Why go to the stock market when in the money market returns are more," said Luz Lorenzo, research head at Peregrine Securities.

To defend the peso from speculative attacks, the Central Bank on Thursday boosted its key overnight borrowing rate by two percentage points to 32 percent. It was the fourth rate rise in just over a week.
Traders said that move largely drove the slide in stocks.
Selling in market heavyweight Philippine Long Distance Telephone shares also helped fuel the tumble in stocks.
Traders blamed the more than $5 overnight fall in PLDT's American Depositary Receipts for the share's losses on the local bourse. PLDT ended 40 pesos lower on Thursday at 850 pesos.
The main index opened 2.68 percent down at 2,519.77 points from Wednesday's close. It hit a new year-low of 2,475.08 points at midsession.
At the end of trading, the market barometer had shed 3.01 percent, or 78.05 points, to 2,511.15, a two-month closing low.
"Certain days you wish you had stayed at home in bed. This was certainly one of those days," said Noel Reyes, vice-president at Anscor Hagedorn Securities.

"It's difficult to say where the stock market is going. The uncertainty for now lies in the hands of the Central Bank. The bottom line is who will be the first to blink, speculators who want the peso to fall or the Central Bank who wants to keep it steady," said a broker from a big foreign brokerage.

The peso came under fresh attack on Wednesday after a Singapore newspaper report quoting a Philippine government minister -- who later said his remarks had been "twisted" -- that the government was considering a devaluation.
The peso was calm in early Thursday trade after the rate rise, trading at 26.40/26.398 to the dollar from the previous close of 26.40.
The Central Bank said it has no plans to devalue the peso but analysts said the market was not convinced.

"The Central Bank is in a 'Catch 22' situation. If they don't defend the peso, it might be devalued. If not, there's only a cost. But as long as the uncertainties are there, the stock market will continue to suffer," said David de la Cruz, vice-president for marketing at Amsteel Securities.

Analysts say much of the speculation stems from fears -- especially among foreign investors -- that the Philippines cannot avoid being infected by the financial crisis in neighbouring Thailand. Last week, the Thai authorities allowed a de facto devaluation of the baht after prolonged speculative pressure.
Most traders in the Philippines expect the share index to test support levels of 2,300 or 2,400 in the short-term. However, some analysts are more optimistic.

"Although there is some lingering fear, there are a lot of good buys. As far as the peso is concerned, we have to be patient. It will come through," Ramon Saulo, senior investment analyst at Asiamerit Securities, said.
